# C++ and QML meet at types {#sec-cpp-qml}

A QML module is the contract between compiled code and views. Register types declaratively,
pass view-specific objects as required inputs, and keep ownership visible.

## Modules name the contract {#sec-qml-modules}

`qt_add_qml_module()` builds QML, C++ registrations, and tooling data together. Static
modules also need their plugin linked into each executable or QML test that imports them.

The module URI is the name QML imports. A class registered with `QML_ELEMENT` or
`QML_NAMED_ELEMENT` becomes a type in that module, and the generated type information lets
`qmllint` and the QML language server check properties and methods. `STATIC` works well for a
module private to one executable; its plugin must be linked as well as the backing library,
or the module's registration can be missing at runtime.

::: {.snippet source="src/app/CMakeLists.txt"}

```cmake
qt_add_qml_module(app_ui
        app.svg\n)
```

:::

## Required properties pass dependencies {#sec-required}

`main()` owns long-lived application objects. It gives QML the objects it needs through
`setInitialProperties()`, and a root component declares matching required properties. This
makes a missing dependency fail while the view loads.

Each page can pass a dependency on to a child using another required property. Types created in
`main()` can declare `QML_UNCREATABLE`, so QML can use their type information but cannot create
an unconnected second instance. This also makes a page straightforward to construct in a test.

The other side of the contract is in `Main.qml`: its root window requires the same typed
properties that `main()` supplies. This adapted excerpt omits the window's visual content:

```qml
ApplicationWindow {
    required property NotificationCenter notifications
    required property SketchbookViewModel sketchbook
    required property CanvasStore canvas
}
```

By contrast, a helper that belongs to one view can be a creatable QML type. QML then creates
and owns an instance for that view. Shared stores and services usually need a longer, explicit
lifetime, which is why the template creates them in `main()`.

::: {.snippet source="src/app/main.cpp"}

```cpp
    engine.setInitialProperties({
    });
```

:::

## Enums and models stay typed {#sec-qml-enums}

Register enums with `Q_ENUM` on a QML type. In QML, enum values are numbers, so annotate
parameters as `int`. For user-visible collections, expose a `QAbstractListModel` rather
than a JavaScript array with copied state.

Sketchbook also exposes the canvas paper background through a registered namespace: `Q_NAMESPACE`
and `Q_ENUM_NS` provide Qt metadata, and QML refers to a value such as `Paper.Dots`. A model's
`roleNames()` gives each piece of row data a name; a delegate declares those roles as required
properties. Precise change signals tell the view which rows to update.

This adapted declaration isolates the enum from the other canvas value types in
[Sketch.hpp](https://github.com/deeedob/qt-kickstart/blob/main/src/canvas/Sketch.hpp):

```cpp
namespace app::canvas {
Q_NAMESPACE
QML_NAMED_ELEMENT(Paper)

enum class PaperBackground { Plain, Dots, Ruled };
Q_ENUM_NS(PaperBackground)
}
```

The canvas settings view can then use `Paper.Dots` when calling the store, instead of relying
on a number whose meaning is unclear. The header belongs to the canvas QML module so the build
can generate its type information.

`SketchListModel::roleNames()` connects the C++ roles to the names QML delegates request:

::: {.snippet source="src/sketchbook/SketchListModel.cpp"}

```cpp
QHash<int, QByteArray> SketchListModel::roleNames() const
        { StrokeCountRole, "strokeCount"_ba },\n    };\n}
```

:::

When a row changes, the model emits `dataChanged()`. For an insertion or removal, it brackets
the mutation with the appropriate begin and end calls. Those signals let a view update the
affected delegates instead of rebuilding its whole list and losing its position.

## Values and identity {#sec-value-types}

Objects and values cross the boundary differently. A `QObject` can have identity, ownership,
and signals. A value such as a number, color, point, or list is passed as a value; changing a
copy does not notify the original property. When the owning property changes, its notify signal
lets a binding read the new value. A model is a better fit for a changing, user-visible list
because it can describe individual row changes.

## Singleton state is rare {#sec-singletons}

Use an external QML singleton only for genuine app-wide state, such as the application
controller. Most state belongs to the view model or store supplied to one screen.

## Lifetimes cross the boundary {#sec-lifetimes}

QML can hold a reference to a C++ object without owning it. An object passed from `main()`
must outlive the QML engine and its views. A QObject returned from an invokable can instead
become QML-owned unless it has a parent, so make ownership explicit when exposing one.

A notification request separates ownership from relevance. The notification center owns
the request object, while its explicit QObject context determines how long the request is
useful. Destroying that context cancels the request, even if a card or dialog is open.
A request that must survive navigation uses a context that survives the page.

Notification actions carry callbacks bound to that same context. Choosing an action finishes
the message once and invokes its callback while the context remains alive. Ordinary callers
do not allocate request objects, connect completion signals or dispatch action IDs.

## Custom rendering has a thread boundary {#sec-custom-items}

Use ordinary QML components when composition is enough. For drawing that needs many custom
shapes, a `QQuickItem` can provide scene graph nodes. Sketchbook's `StrokeItem` does this for
strokes. The scene graph can run on a render thread, so synchronize item state at Qt's
rendering boundary and do not touch GUI objects from that thread.

`updatePaintNode()` is the point where an item updates scene graph nodes. Qt calls it during
scene graph synchronization while the GUI thread is blocked, so the item can transfer the
state needed for rendering. The returned nodes belong to the scene graph and may be reused on
later frames. Do not treat that synchronization window as permission to access GUI objects
freely from other render-thread code.

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [Qt Quick scene graph](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtquick-visualcanvas-scenegraph.html)
and [C++ and QML ownership](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtqml-cppintegration-data.html#data-ownership).
:::
